argument: Through Notes from Underground, Dostoevsky attacks the utopian socialist faith that rationality can fully explain people and organize them into a crystal palace, insisting that the actual internal experience of a human being is chaotic, contradictory, and irrational. His Underground Man is a very smart person who sees through every illusion yet cannot escape a double-bind: he can neither deny the stone wall of rational truth nor accept that rationality can predict or coordinate human experience, leaving him in a contemplative inertia that Nishitani diagnoses as a negated self stuck in the field of nihility. The episodes with his former classmates and with Liza show what this imprisonment costs him, since equating freedom with independence only makes him alone, and Liza's unconditional love threatens the transactional worldview that keeps him safe, while love, suffering, and confession, all activities rooted in self-emptying, remain the uncomfortable experiences that could actually transform him.
keyIdeas: Dostoevsky rejects the utopian crystal palace vision of thinkers like Chernyshevsky and Fourier because it treats people as rational calculators to be ordered like piano keys, denying the chaotic, contradictory internal experience of actually being a person.

The Underground Man is clearly very smart, which matters because his prison was built not by stupidity but by seeing through illusions, undercutting the idea that bad lives come from insufficient reasoning.

His contemplative inertia comes from an exact double-bind: he cannot deny the stone wall where two times two equals four, but he also cannot accept rationality as able to fully predict or coordinate human experience, so he can never affirm or act on anything.

Nishitani reads him as a negated self stuck in the field of nihility, neither dead nor alive, in reactionary inactivity, and respects him, and Dostoevsky, precisely because this is a nihilism deeper than the atheist-and-fan-of-science kind, one that questions the foundations of rationality itself.

Dostoevsky argues that being independent is a synonym for being alone rather than free, and that unconditional love, like Liza's, terrifies the Underground Man because it falsifies his transactional worldview; love, suffering, and confession are all self-emptying activities whose discomfort people avoid, thereby avoiding the transformation they could bring.

terms.def: Fourier's image for the rationally ordered utopia in which social science has resolved human disputes and imbalances, the utopian socialist vision Dostoevsky finds ridiculous.

Dostoevsky's name for the things that seem rationally, objectively true and deterministic, like two times two equals four, which the Underground Man can neither deny nor accept as the full truth of experience.
The limbo of endless doubting and contemplation without action that traps someone who can neither deny nor accept rationality.
Nishitani's field of awareness in which the stable forms that give meaning to reality are called into question, the field the Underground Man is overly stuck in as its human embodiment.
Love understood not as a set of conditions being met but as a commitment and process of accepting a whole person in all their complexity, in contrast to conditional, utilitarian love.
The removal of the ways you project yourself onto someone or something to make room for receiving them as they are, which love, suffering, and confession are all rooted in.
